tier_reason: Enricher: C stands; caveats corrected (source and numbers mismatch, relabelled Java flag, integer overflow).

corrections.caveats: From 2009 with Apple g++ 4.0.1 targeting 32-bit i686 (-march=pentium4) on a Xeon against a 64-bit HotSpot VM, so the targets differ; no PGO or modern speculative devirtualisation for C++. One call site (400 million alternating virtual calls incrementing a global), not a general claim. The published C++ source does not match the numbers: the latest revision of gist 87516 shows five bench() calls (without semicolons) while the results list ten C++ timings, which most likely come from an earlier 10-iteration revision. The Java numbers were first posted under 'java Bench -J-Server' (the flag passed to Bench as an ignored argument) and later relabelled 'java -server Bench' (cosmetic: already a 64-bit Server VM). The C++ static int counter overflows INT_MAX in the third call (UB). The mechanism is probably bimorphic inlining (about 11.6 vs 5 cycles per iteration, derived from page data).

The author's a-warning.md (2015-08-18) calls the benchmark misleading: hard-coded text, small dictionary, pre-split words, no allocation cost. The gap comes from LuaJIT's interned, pre-hashed string keys against the C version's first-character hash with strcmp chains and libstdc++ std::unordered_map overhead, not from JIT versus AOT; the 10x rerun (0.76 vs 1.44 s) rules out start-up cost, and the 'optimizes away all dictionary lookups' remark was never checked with -jdump (about 4-8.5 ns per word fits one real interned-key lookup). In the thread, ayosec's Rust 0.104 s ran 100,000 passes against C's 1,000,000 (10x less work) and marcomagdy's pointer-keyed unordered_map still took 0.495 s against LuaJIT's 0.186 s. test.c uses implicit int, so it fails to build on GCC 14+ and Clang 16+ by default. No licence; single `time` runs.

tier_reason: Enricher: C stands; -L has a Word64 underflow on backspace and the GNU wc baseline predates the coreutils 9.x speedups; caveats corrected.

corrections.caveats: Numbers are a single ratio sentence in the README with no hardware, file size, GNU wc version, locale or timing method; the author's Habr article and blog post could not be opened. hwc does less work than GNU wc: ASCII-only whitespace for words, characters counted as non-continuation bytes without UTF-8 validation, output format not wc's. Correctness bug in -L: the backspace rule max 0 (curLen - 1) on Word64 underflows, so a backspace followed by a line end or EOF reports 18446744073709551615 and '\babc' gives 2 where GNU wc 8.32 gives 3 (simulated in Python; hwc not run here). -l alone runs bytestring's C fps_count loop and -c alone is O(1), as in GNU. The baseline is stale: coreutils 9.0 made -l up to 5x faster with AVX2, 9.5 calls wc much faster, and 9.11 sped up -m 2.6x on non-ASCII UTF-8. Pinned to GHC 8.8 with the LLVM backend; abandoned since 2020-03-15.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README table (one timed run each) against the macOS system /usr/bin/sort labelled 'GNU sort (system)': 1M lines -n 1.00 vs 0.03 s (33.3x); 1M text 0.57 vs 0.03 (19.0x); 1M -rn 0.95 vs 0.03; 10M -n 6.21 vs 0.45 (13.8x); 10M text 6.00 vs 0.43 (14.0x); 10M -f 8.09 vs 0.42 (19.3x); 10M -g 24.17 vs 2.24; 10M -u 2.50 vs 0.55; 10M -s 3.28 vs 0.55. The 10M -f row timed a plain byte sort (see caveats) and the -n and -rn rows run paths that misorder or reverse their output, so only the plain text rows against the BSD sort stand.
corrections.caveats: Baseline mislabelled: the 'GNU sort (system)' column is Apple's BSD-derived macOS sort (benchmark.sh defaults to the system sort and its own usage text names /usr/bin/sort BSD and gsort GNU); eBay tsv-utils reports current GNU sort often more than twice as fast as the macOS sort and uutils sort beats the same column by about 8x at 10M lines. Harness flaw by code reading: files over 100 MiB go through external_sort.rs, which passes only the numeric and unique flags, and the 10M-line strings file is 138.9 MB, so the 10M -f row (0.42 s vs 0.43 s for plain text) timed a plain byte sort and the '19x case-insensitive' headline is invalid. Correctness bugs: -r without -k is reversed twice outside the numeric path (ascending output); -n's radix path validates only the first 100 lines and then uses an unvalidated byte - b'0' (wraps in release), misordering later decimal or text lines; -nu and -fu dedupe by exact bytes; the external merge's double-reversed heap emits unsorted output; multi-file merge ignores -n, -r, -f and -u; stdin is silently truncated at 2 GB. Issue #1: 92 GB RSS and OOM on 1.5 TB input. One run per cell, macOS 15.5, no CPU model.

tier_reason: Enricher: the measured queries run a matcher that gives different answers from jq (key text matched anywhere without a colon check, neq true if any occurrence differs, single-field aggregates that drop values) and the JSON re-formatting row emits invalid JSON for many inputs, on top of first-party numbers with no script, dataset or CPU; no like-for-like measurement against jq remains: D.

corrections.caveats: First-party only: no CPU, benchmark script, dataset, baseline versions or flags, and jq and jaq share one column. zog does different and weaker work than jq: it does not parse or validate JSON, ignores nesting, matches numbers literally and assumes single-line UTF-8 JSONL. Correctness bugs in the measured code (src/scanner.zig, present at benchmarked commit 7e83065): the WHERE matcher accepts any occurrence of the quoted key text with no colon check (`error exists` matches {"level":"error"}) and neq is true if any occurrence differs; --format json leaves strings unquoted when the first byte is a digit, '-', 't', 'f' or 'n' and truncates objects and arrays, so the JSON re-formatting row is not equivalent to jq; single-field SELECT and aggregates can return an empty value (sum undercounts); unchecked i64 overflow on 19+ digit integers; lines over 8 MiB end the scan. README numbers date from 2026-02-27, before the Zig 0.16 std.Io port (v1.0.0 unmeasured); the Linux release is built for baseline x86-64 (SSE2, not AVX2).

tier_reason: Enricher: C stands; caveats corrected (prefix-extraction bug in the index, -c and chunk paths; parallelism behind the wins).

corrections.caveats: Very new (crate first published 2026-03-04), first-party numbers on a small synthetic corpus (about 1M lines; runs of 4-85 ms including process start-up). The win is mostly 12-thread parallelism against single-threaded GNU grep: --no-index is faster than the default warm-index mode in 4 of the 5 indexed rows and the index helps only on the very sparse query; GNU grep wins -rl 'fn main' (7.12 vs 7.50 ms). Correctness bug in src/pattern.rs extract_literal_prefix: it keeps the character before a ?, * or { quantifier, so colou?r gets the required prefix 'colou' and https?:// gets 'https'; that prefix drives the warm-index file filter, the -c count path and the over-4-MiB parallel chunk path, which only look at lines containing it, so lines with only 'color' or 'http://' are missed. The benchmarked patterns do not use those quantifiers.

tier_reason: Enricher: the markdup baseline in guigolab/sambamBench-nf ran single-threaded because the samtools template drops the '$' from '-@{task.cpus}', the sambamba view 1.47x row is a cold-cache artefact and the warm 4.88x row has no counters, and the README's '2x faster at 120GB+' compares sambamba with itself. Crippled-baseline precedent: B to C.

corrections.caveats: The markdup baseline is crippled: the samtools-1.7 template does two full sorts plus fixmate before markdup, and its sort and fixmate steps pass '-@{task.cpus}' without the '$' (the resolved script in report_16_120G.html shows the literal), so samtools ran at 102% CPU against 658-890% for sambamba; the 4.49x and 3.62x markdup wins are against a single-threaded four-stage pipeline. The first task (sambamba 0.6.8-pre1 view) read 4.59 GB cold from disk while every later task read under 4 MB, so its 52.8 s (1.47x) is a cold-cache artefact and the warm 0.6.6 view row (4.88x) has no CPU or I/O counters. The README's sort claim (up to 2x faster at 120GB+) is sambamba against itself (stats.org, 20 GB vs 120 GB) and the 120 GB report has samtools 1.7 sorting 1.70x faster; issue #447: the maintainer recommends samtools sort except on high-RAM machines. samtools 1.7 was built at -O2 with plain zlib (no libdeflate before htslib 1.8). The CRG report behind the README could not be opened.

tier_reason: Enricher: B stands (Nature Methods 2023 paper and public skani-test harness); caveats corrected.

corrections.caveats: The speedup is algorithmic, not a language effect: skani does approximate mapping with sparse chaining of k-mer seeds and no base-level alignment, while FastANI maps 3 kb fragments, so the Rust-vs-C++ question is not answered; skani is slower than Mash at querying (16x on D3, 6x on the 195-MAG triangle). The committed time_2328_results.sh sets threads=1 but the checked-in times ran at -t 50, so the script does not reproduce them; FastANI --rl/--ql runs both directions of each pair while skani triangle runs each once (about 2x of the 54x); the RefSeq 750x uses triangle -E with the marker screen, and skani search mode took 174.8 s (about 61x). The v0.4 '2x faster' is PR #58's self-measured 1.41-1.61x at the default c=125 (1.91x only at c=30) with hardware unstated. Default ANI passes through a learned GBDT model whose output is piecewise constant (issue #57); the timings come from the paper-era binary, not the current release.

tier_reason: Enricher: C stands; the samtools depth baseline predates its 2021 pileup-free rewrite, and the table predates two mosdepth correctness fixes; caveats corrected.

corrections.caveats: The README table lists no hardware, tool versions or commands; the Bioinformatics 2018 paper was not opened. Stale baseline: the 2x is against pileup-based samtools depth (2017; the table predates --fast-mode, v0.2.4 of 2018-11-19). samtools 1.13 (July 2021, PR #1428) rewrote depth without pileup, 3.3x faster than 1.11 on a 30-50x BAM (19.755 s vs 6.049 s) and 33x on deep CRAM, and was never re-compared with mosdepth. Output asymmetry: per-position text vs run-length bgzipped BED plus index. The table predates fixes 0.2.2 (wrong values on same-length chromosomes) and 0.2.5 (full mate-overlap double count). Both tools decode through htslib; mosdepth's documented build links libdeflate. Fast mode counts D/N spans as covered; the median is clamped at 65,535 and the histogram at 400,000; open #268 (CRAM 3.1 static-binary decode failure).

tier_reason: Enricher: C stands; parity port whose small wins mostly time the C API's per-call allocation; caveats corrected.

corrections.caveats: A parity result, not a clear win: the README says the crate 'should roughly match' C++ Snappy on x86_64, and snap is faster on about half the rows (up to 1.10x) and slower on others (uflat04_pdf C++ 1.10x faster). The C++ side is the system Snappy 1.1.8 dylib (distribution build flags) called through the C API over FFI, whose compress path heap-allocates WorkingMemory on every call and whose wrapper parses the length header twice on decompress, while snap uses an inline 1,024-entry table, so the 8-10% jpg_200 wins (10-25 ns) mostly measure per-call overhead. Snappy 1.1.9 to 1.3.1 were never measured. Tree Borrows UB in read_copy (#56) was fixed in 1.1.1.

tier_reason: Enricher: C stands; the benchmarked runs used the default early-EOF shortcut that is unsafe on network file systems; caveats corrected.

corrections.caveats: The numbers are one-line source comments with no machine, kernel, file system, cache state, tool versions, Nim flags or script; ranges without raw timings, dating from 2020 and covering only the portable path (the -d:batch mode adds about 1.25x per commit 2948a0d). Early-EOF shortcut is on by default (eof0=false sets eeof=true): a short getdents read ends the directory, which the source says fails on sshfs and NFS; commit 7559cff (2020-06-28) turned the old opt-in -d:dentsLocalFS into this default, so the benchmarked find and ls runs used it, and bu du hard-codes eof0=false. EMFILE/ENFILE silently ends a subtree (depth capped by ulimit -n). Commit ebb78e9 only added '|fd' to the old '1.7x faster than FreeBSD find' comment with no separate fd number. By code reading: ls1AU and lss1AU print in post-order and lss1AU headers show the parent directory via libc dirname (outputs went to /dev/null); bu du -p uses 1 shl 40, --exclude does not prune, and StatxTs < and <= compare tv_nsec with tv_sec.

tier_reason: Enricher: C stands; the pkill ratio was never timed and the pgrep side is hard-coded; caveats corrected.

corrections.caveats: The gains come from doing less work: pd -f%p %c reads only /proc/PID/stat and prints the pid and the 15-character comm, while /bin/ps ax prints PID, TTY, STAT, TIME and the full argv and procps also parses /proc/PID/status, so the outputs differ. bench.sh never times pkill: the README's '(5.745 +- 0.016)X slower than pk' is the i7-1370P pgrep row over the mean of pf's first-hit and no-match times, and the equal-work ratios are 3.75x (i7-6700K) and 4.12x (i7-1370P). The pgrep side is hard-coded 'pgrep -x init' while pf uses the first /proc entry's comm, so the script breaks on systemd hosts; pf matches with an unanchored PCRE and has no -x mode. In bench.sh -e1 means --exist --first (exit at the first match with no output).

tier_reason: Enricher: D stands (refuted claim); the opened benchmark measured Caddy over HTTP/2 against nginx over HTTP/1.1 without upstream keepalive, and the tuned nginx still won; caveats corrected.

corrections.caveats: Recorded as an unsupported and contradicted claim. The 4x figure is only an HN submission title; the post could not be opened, so its method, versions and configs are unknown. In the opened benchmark (11 stars, no license, 'quick-and-dirty' by its own description) the first nginx.conf had worker_connections 1024 and no sendfile, access_log or upstream HTTP/1.1 settings; in every run Vegeta sent HTTP/2 to Caddy (offered by ALPN) and HTTP/1.1 to nginx ('listen 443 ssl' without http2), and the nginx upstream block has no keepalive directive, so nginx opened a new backend TCP connection per request while Caddy reused pooled ones. Both asymmetries favour Caddy, and the tuned nginx still won.
